misconceptions.say: On dropping `std::atomic`: that does not address sharing, it removes the synchronisation that makes the counts correct in the first place. Two threads incrementing a plain `long` is a data race, and a data race is undefined behaviour no matter how the cache behaves.

On the memory order: a weaker order changes what the compiler and the CPU may reorder around the increment. It does not change which cache line the two counters sit in, and false sharing is a question about addresses.

feedback.nudge: False sharing happens when two hot variables land in the same cache line. Ask of each option in turn: does it change where those variables live, or how often they are touched? Anything that changes neither cannot help.

distractors.0: Correct. `alignas(64)` forces each counter onto its own 64-byte boundary, so they land in different lines and the two cores stop fighting. `std::hardware_destructive_interference_size` is the portable spelling of that 64. The cost is size: the struct grows from 16 bytes to 128.
distractors.1: Correct, and this is the better fix. A thread-local accumulator is not shared at all, so there is nothing to keep coherent — the hot loop becomes a register increment, which is not merely faster than a ping-ponging line but faster than an uncontended atomic too. One atomic add per thread at the end is free by comparison. This is what a reduction is, and it is why every parallel framework offers one.
distractors.2: No — and it makes things worse, not better. Dropping `atomic` removes the synchronisation, which is now a data race and undefined behaviour, so the counts can simply be wrong. It does not help the speed either: coherence is maintained by the hardware per line regardless of what the source says, so two plain `long`s in one line ping-pong exactly as much. False sharing is not caused by atomics; atomics only make it easy to measure.
distractors.3: No. `relaxed` removes the memory *fences* around the increment, which does help a little on some architectures, but the line still has to be owned exclusively by a core to be written to. The ping-pong is the coherence protocol doing its job, and no ordering relaxation can avoid it — an exclusive write needs the line. Expect a modest gain here and nothing like the 30x you are missing.

explanation:
## The two real fixes: pad it, or stop sharing it

Options 0 and 1. The other two change the source without changing which cache line each counter lives in, and the line is the only thing that matters.

## Why it costs 30x

Coherence is maintained **per line**, not per variable. For a core to write to a line it must hold that line in the Exclusive or Modified state, which means invalidating every other core's copy. So on each increment:

1. Core 1 wants the line to write `a`. It sends an invalidate; core 2 drops its copy.
2. Core 2 wants the line to write `b`. It sends an invalidate; core 1 drops its copy.
3. Repeat, ten million times.

Each round trip is an L3 or interconnect transaction, tens to low hundreds of cycles, where an L1 hit is about four. The two cores are doing nothing but passing one 64-byte line back and forth — and *nothing is actually shared*. Neither thread ever reads the other's number. The sharing is entirely an artefact of layout, which is what makes it "false".

## Padding: correct, and the cost is obvious

```cpp
struct Counters {
    alignas(64) std::atomic<long> a;
    alignas(64) std::atomic<long> b;
};
```

`sizeof(Counters)` goes from 16 to 128. Each counter now owns a line, so the cores never contend. Use `std::hardware_destructive_interference_size` rather than a literal 64 if you want it portable — that constant exists in `<new>` precisely for this.

This is the right fix when the counters genuinely must be shared and updated often — a per-core statistics array, a work-stealing deque's head and tail, a spinlock next to the data it protects. Note the direction of the lesson for arrays: `alignas(64) std::atomic<long> counters[N]` makes an array where every element is in its own line, which is exactly what you want for per-thread counters and a 8x memory increase you should be deliberate about.

## Not sharing at all: better, when you can

```cpp
long local = 0;
for (...) local++;            // a register, no memory traffic at all
shared.a.fetch_add(local);    // once
```

This is faster than the padded version, not just faster than the broken one. The padded version still does ten million atomic read-modify-writes to memory; this does ten million register increments and one atomic. An uncontended `lock xadd` is still ~20 cycles against ~1 for an `inc` on a register.

The general shape is a **reduction**: compute privately, combine once. OpenMP's `reduction(+:sum)`, `std::reduce`, and every map-reduce framework are this idea. When you find false sharing, the first question is not "how do I pad it" but "why is this shared at all".

## How to find it

False sharing is invisible in the source — the code looks like two independent variables, because it *is* two independent variables. You find it with hardware counters:

```bash
perf stat -e cache-misses,cache-references ./prog
perf c2c record ./prog && perf c2c report    # built for exactly this
```

`perf c2c` ("cache to cache") exists specifically to attribute line contention to source lines. The symptom that should make you reach for it: **a parallel program that gets slower as you add threads**, with no lock in the hot path to blame.

## One thing it is not

False sharing is not a correctness bug. The counts in the original program are right — `std::atomic` guarantees that. It is purely a performance pathology, which is why it survives code review so easily and why the only way to catch it is to measure.
